newsitem.title: KENYA: Police beat rioting students in central Nairobi.
newsitem.headline: Police beat rioting students in central Nairobi.

text.p: Thousands of Kenyan students fought riot police in the heart of Nairobi on Monday, defying President Daniel arap Moi a week after the worst political unrest in Kenya in seven years.

The Kenya Polytechnic students seized control for hours of Haile Selassie Avenue, a major highway through the city centre, throwing stones and demanding constitutional reforms before parliamentary and presidential elections later this year.
"Moi must go, Moi must go," chanted the students in addition to: "The time for change is now" and "We want reforms now".
Witnesses said two people, who were apparently passersby, were seriously injured. Riot police wielding batons badly beat two youths, who looked like students, lying on the ground.
The youths bled from their heads as they were repeatedly hit. Several policemen using batons lashed one on a rubbish heap before walking off but one policeman only returned to beat him again.
Moments later, a riot policeman knocked Reuters photographer George Mulala unconscious by hitting him on the head with a baton. He was released from Nairobi hospital after treatment.

Riot and crack General Service Unit (GSU) police fired teargas and rubber bullets to drive the students back into the polytechnic campus after they hit police and cars with rocks and used slingshots to send stones flying across the wide avenue.
Hundreds of police later stormed the campus firing live ammunition in the air and teargas and retook the highway.
Police reported no police casualties. Several woman students screamed as they were beaten during the police charge on campus.
The violence in the city centre broke out a week after nine people were killed during unrest in Nairobi and other towns and cities and fierce clashes between demonstrators and riot police.
Students blocked almost the entire length of the avenue with tyres and makeshift barricades set ablaze. GSU units secured the Central Bank and riot police protected the nearby U.S. embassy.
Some students also shouted slogans against Asians, accusing Kenyans of Asian origin of growing rich at their expense.
But the unrest failed to halt business in Nairobi as it was confined to Haile Selassie Avenue. Elsewhere, traffic snarled up in places but most people went on with their work as usual.
Opposition-backed groups have campaigned since June for Moi to agree to constitutional reforms before presidential and parliamentary elections this year. No date is set for the polls.

Moi, 73 and in power for the last 19 years, said last Friday he would take action against any attempt to bring chaos to the country and challenged the opposition to take the debate on reforms to parliament, where his ruling party has a majority.
Authorities ordered Nairobi University and Jomo Kenyatta University closed indefinitely last week and students sent home following days of clashes with riot police in the capital.
In addition to the reform issue, students are angered by a draft parliamentary bill requiring the expulsion of those who fail to pay fees. The bill is a World Bank condition for aid.
Anglican Archbishop David Gitari on Sunday verbally attacked Moi from the pulpit at Nairobi's All Saints Cathedral at a ceremonial "cleansing" and re-dedication after riots last week.
Police threw teargas into the cathedral and beat opposition and reform leaders when people fleeing a confrontation between demonstrators and police sought refuge there last Monday.
Moslem preacher Sheikh Khalid Balala, one of Moi's main opponents, was at the service after being allowed by authorities back into Kenya on Saturday from two years' exile in Germany.
